content: Bronchiolitis is the most prevalent lower respiratory tract infection in children aged between 1 month and 2 years. It is primarily caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and is marked by inflammation, swelling, and necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium. Histologically, bronchiolitis can be categorized into bronchiolitis obliterans, proliferative bronchiolitis, diffuse panbronchiolitis, or respiratory bronchiolitis. The Bronchiolitis Severity Score (BSS) is used to classify the disease into four severity levels. Clinically, it presents with symptoms such as rhinitis, cough, wheezing, crackles (rales), use of accessory respiratory muscles, and nasal flaring. In infants, risk factors include being younger than 6 months, lack of breastfeeding, prematurity, and congenital heart disease. The cornerstone of treatment is supportive care. Bronchiolitis was first identified in 1899 by researchers at the University of Minnesota and was fully described in 1901 by Dr. Lange. The disease is classified based on the patient’s age and histological features. It is divided into adult and infant bronchiolitis by age. Histologically, it is further classified into acute infectious bronchiolitis, bronchiolitis obliterans, proliferative bronchiolitis, diffuse panbronchiolitis, and respiratory bronchiolitis. The Bronchiolitis Severity Score (BSS) is used to stratify the disease into four classes. The disease is transmitted via airborne droplets. RSV infects the nasopharyngeal mucosa and subsequently spreads to the lower respiratory tract, where it replicates in the bronchioles. This viral infection triggers inflammation, leading to edema and necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium. Increased vascular permeability results in edema and swelling. Histopathologically, bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized by intraluminal polyps, inflammatory infiltration, and macrophages, while constrictive bronchiolitis shows airway thickening and luminal narrowing. Bronchiolitis predominantly affects children under 2 years of age, with a peak incidence between 3 and 6 months. RSV is the most common causative agent, but other viruses such as adenovirus, influenza, and parainfluenza can also be responsible. Bacterial pathogens like Legionella pneumophila and Mycoplasma pneumoniae may also cause bronchiolitis. It is essential to differentiate bronchiolitis from other respiratory and cardiac conditions with similar presentations, such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pneumonia, congestive heart failure, tuberculosis, pertussis, foreign body aspiration, pulmonary embolism, and diffuse idiopathic neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia. Bronchiolitis is one of the most common acute respiratory illnesses in infants and children, affecting approximately 3,000 per 100,000 children in the United States. It is most prevalent during the fall, winter, and early spring months. While it can affect individuals of all ages, it primarily impacts infants under 2 years of age, with a higher incidence in boys than girls. Native American, Alaskan, and Hispanic populations are disproportionately affected. Despite the high hospitalization rates, the mortality rate is low. Risk factors for bronchiolitis vary by age. In infants, risk factors include being younger than 6 months, lack of breastfeeding, prematurity, and congenital heart disease. If untreated, bronchiolitis typically begins with mild upper respiratory symptoms, shortness of breath, wheezing, persistent cough, and rapid breathing (tachypnea) within the first 2–3 days. By days 3–7, chest wall retractions and nasal flaring may develop. Symptoms usually resolve within two weeks. Complications are more likely in infants younger than 2 months, premature infants, and those with underlying conditions such as congenital heart disease, chronic pulmonary disease, or immunodeficiencies. Prognosis can be estimated using severity scores. The diagnosis of bronchiolitis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination. Common symptoms include fever, cough, difficulty breathing (dyspnea), and nasal discharge. Other symptoms may include post-tussive vomiting and dehydration. On physical examination, patients may appear toxic or cyanotic. Fever may or may not be present. Lung examination often reveals intercostal and substernal retractions, wheezing, crackles, and diminished breath sounds. Extrapulmonary manifestations, such as pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, arrhythmias, tachycardia, and seizures, may also occur. Laboratory tests are not specific for bronchiolitis but may include viral pathogen tests such as ELISA, immunofluorescent assays, and optical immunoassays. Complete blood count and pulmonary function tests may help support the diagnosis and rule out other obstructive lung diseases. Chest X-rays are nonspecific and may show findings such as atelectasis and consolidations. They are primarily used to exclude other conditions like pneumonia. CT scans may reveal centrilobular nodules, bronchiolar wall thickening, ground-glass opacities, and parenchymal cysts, but these findings are nonspecific. MRI and other imaging modalities do not provide additional diagnostic value for bronchiolitis. The primary treatment for bronchiolitis is supportive care. This includes frequent small feedings and oxygen therapy. In severe cases, intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding may be required. Prophylaxis with palivizumab is recommended for high-risk infants, such as those with significant congenital heart disease or preterm infants requiring oxygen for at least the first 28 days of life. Surgical intervention is not indicated for bronchiolitis. During RSV season, passive immunization with palivizumab is recommended for high-risk patients.
